facts.label: legend
facts.quote: In folk versions of the story, the royal family of Gandhara is imprisoned and starved by Dhritarashtra, prompting Subala to sacrifice the family so Shakuni could survive to avenge them.
facts.text: A popular regional folklore tradition claims that Dhritarashtra imprisoned and starved the Gandharan royal family on a single grain of rice per day, choosing Shakuni to survive so he could destroy the Kuru lineage from within.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Eventually, when the king died, Shakuni used his bones to make a pair of dice. The dice were magical and obeyed Shakuni's command.
facts.text: Folklore retellings maintain that Shakuni's dice were supernatural artifacts fashioned out of the thigh or spine bone of his dying father King Subala, ensuring the rolls always matched Shakuni's spoken will.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Plain discs were recovered from the levels of Hastinapura II and were regarded as gaming counters.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India (Ancient India, Nos. 10 & 11)
facts.text: Excavations carried out by the Archaeological Survey of India at Hastinapura between 1950 and 1952 yielded terracotta gaming discs and counters from Period II strata associated with the Painted Grey Ware period.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The excavations at Taxila carried out between 1913 and 1934 revealed the stratigraphical sequence of the Gandharan capital from the earliest settlements at Bhir Mound.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India (Taxila Excavation Memoir)
facts.text: Excavations conducted by Sir John Marshall for the Archaeological Survey of India at Taxila between 1913 and 1934 revealed stratified urban settlements of the ancient Gandhara kingdom dating from the sixth century BCE onward.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Scholars differ on whether the revenge motif of Shakuni stems from vernacular folk traditions such as Terukkuttu and Nautanki or was invented by modern dramatic and television adaptations.
facts.text: Literary historians dispute whether the sympathetic revenge motivation for Shakuni originated in medieval vernacular folk theatre or emerged primarily through twentieth-century stage adaptations and mass media dramatizations.
